name: Kikongo-Kituba
catalog_citation: Mufwene, Salikoko S. 2013. Survey chapter: Kikongo-Kituba. In Michaelis, Maurer, Haspelmath & Huber (eds.), The Survey of Pidgin and Creole Languages / APiCS Online, survey 58. https://apics-online.info/surveys/58
catalog_locator: Section 3 'Phonology', final three paragraphs (tone/accent); Section 6 'Closure' (penultimate pitch-accent remark)
catalog_quote: Kikongo-Kituba has a predominantly fixed accent system, with the accent/tone borne by the penultimate syllable, as in any of its names. The majority of the words have only one accent (high tone) borne by the penultimate syllable (e.g. dísù HL ‘eye’, kwísà HL ‘come.IMP’, kàpítà LHL ‘foreman’, bábà HL ‘mute’). Derivative words and conjugated verbs are especially subject to this accent/tone placement rule, e.g. kù-sál-à LHL ‘to work’ ... kù-pés-à LHL ‘give’ > kù-pès-íl-à LLHL ‘give on the behalf, or for the benefit, of’. However, Kikongo-Kituba also has a significant proportion of polysyllabic words either with only low tones (e.g. mùntù LL ‘person’, mùnòkò LLL ‘mouth, opening’, dìkùlù LLL ‘leg, foot’, mbàlà LL ‘time’ as in ‘five times’) or with a high tone on the last syllable or on both the penultimate and last syllables (e.g. nzìlá LH ‘way, road’, mbàlá LH ‘yam’, dìlálá LHH ‘citrus frui…
sweep_summary: One bibliography item (Ngalasso 1991, Études Créoles 14(2): 147-162) — a dedicated 16-page first-hand study of the tone/accent question in exactly this variety (eastern Kituba of Bandundu, Zaire/DRC). Full text already fetched sources by a prior pass (Persée PDF is altcha-gated; the 16 page images and their scanned are; I read the whole scanned and verified the key passages against the page images (pp. 148, 159, 160), and wrote. Ngalasso confirms the catalog's 'tonal' coding (the variety 'est toujours une langue à tons au sens le plus strict du terme', with minimal pairs and six lexical tonal schemes) and refines Mufwene 2013's 'accent/tone on the penultimate' statement: the canonical scheme I has H on the first root syllable (penult only in short words), other schemes are lexically contrastive, and an independent dynamic (length) accent falls on the first root syllable 'quel que soit le schème tonal', 'pas automatiquement sur la pénultième'; the penult-rise reading is called a superficial impression (while conceded for Brazzaville/Boma-Matadi broadcast speech). Best new statement: p. 159 'L'accent du kikongo' (quoted); it is a stronger first-hand source than the short APiCS survey chapter for the 'tonal' verdict and adds a root-initial stress locus, so it can supersede or at least co-decide the record; catalog kind stays 'tonal'. The FSI Kituba Basic Course (Swift & Zola 1963, on file from the prior pass, not in the item list) states 'accent on the root syllable and pitch rise on the next to the last syllable' as the normal pattern (p. xv), consistent with Ngalasso. Nothing left to acquire for this item.

new_statements.quote: K. E. Laman (1936) l'avait déjà noté : l'énergie articulatoire caractéristique de l'accent dynamique du kikongo se localise en un point très précis à l'intérieur de l'unité lexicale : généralement sa place se trouve sur la première syllabe de la racine, quel que soit par ailleurs le schème tonal. Cette règle semble toujours en vigueur en kikongo véhiculaire. L'accent est particulièrement perceptible dans les formes prononcées avec une grande insistance : la voyelle accentuée a tendance à être prononcée plus longue que les autres. Les exemples qui suivent montrent clairement 1° que l'accent ne se confond pas systématiquement avec un ton haut ; 2° que sa place n'est pas automatiquement sur la pénultième.
new_statements.translation: K. E. Laman (1936) had already noted it: the articulatory energy characteristic of the dynamic accent of Kikongo is localised at a very precise point within the lexical unit: generally its place is on the first syllable of the root, whatever the tonal scheme. This rule seems still to be in force in vehicular Kikongo. The accent is particularly perceptible in forms pronounced with great insistence: the accented vowel tends to be pronounced longer than the others. The examples that follow show clearly 1° that the accent does not systematically coincide with a high tone; 2° that its place is not automatically on the penultimate syllable.
new_statements.citation: Ngalasso, Mwatha Musanji. 1991. Tons ou accents ? Analyse des schèmes tonals du kikongo parlé dans la région de Bandundu (Zaïre). Études Créoles 14(2): 147-162. doi:10.3406/ecreo.1991.1369
new_statements.locator: p. 159, section 'L'accent du kikongo', first paragraph (thesis restated p. 148 and in the Conclusion p. 160)
new_statements.reading: Eastern (Bandundu/DRC) Kituba keeps lexical tone (H/L + falling; minimal pairs; six lexical tonal schemes, of which the canonical scheme I puts H on the first root syllable, which is the penult only in di- and trisyllables) AND has an independent, non-contrastive dynamic accent (mainly length) fixed on the first syllable of the root/lexical base. The catalog's 'tonal' kind is confirmed; Mufwene's 'accent/tone borne by the penultimate syllable' is refined: the H of the canonical scheme is root-initial rather than penult-counting, other schemes (all-L, final-H, prefix-H, BHH) are lexically contrastive, and the stress proper is root-initial, not penultimate.

new_statements.second_reader_bearing_note: Catalog kind 'tonal' (TONAL-OR-PITCH-ACCENT) stands and is strengthened: Ngalasso 1991 gives lexical minimal pairs (p. 150: kudíla 'profiter de' / kudila 'pleurer', mbála 'patate douce' / mbala 'fois', mukánda 'livre' / mukandá 'peau' / mukanda 'circoncision', etc.), six lexical tonal schemes incl. all-L (III), final-H (II), prefix-H (IV), BHH (V), HBH (VI) (pp. 152-158), and concludes (p. 160) that the eastern Bandundu variety is still a tone language, tone and accent coexisting. audit.action: cite a better source for the same coding
audit.reasoning: (1) Quote check: the deciding quotation and the exceptions quotation are verbatim in the held APiCS survey 58 text at the stated places (Section 3 Phonology, final paragraphs; Section 6 Closure). (2) Deciding source: a 2013 peer-reviewed survey sketch by the foremost Kituba specialist; short, but first-hand and tone-marked. (3) Better/other sources: the one dedicated prosody article (Ngalasso 1991, Études Créoles) and the 470-pp FSI course (Swift & Zola 1963) were both fetched sources now into FSI pp. xv-xvi: default pattern = length-accent on root syllable plus pitch rise on the penult, with a lexical class of even/low-pitched (Lingala-cognate) words and French loans with non-penult pitch - the same picture as Mufwene. Ngalasso pp. 148-160: Kituba (Bandundu) remains a tone language with six lexical tone schemes; the penult-H scheme I is canoni

sources.citation: Ngalasso, Mwatha Musanji. 1991. Tons ou accents ? Analyse des schèmes tonals du kikongo parlé dans la région de Bandundu (Zaïre). Études Créoles 14(2): 147-162. doi:10.3406/ecreo.1991.1369 (Persée; PDF is altcha-gated, so the 16 page images were fetched sources and scanned, eng+fra)
sources.quote: p.148: the eastern (Bandundu) variety 'est toujours une langue à tons au sens le plus strict du terme'; tones 'coexistent avec un système accentuel dont la forme ne coïncide pas toujours avec une intonation haute et dont la fonction linguistique est marginale'; 'l'idée d'une montée de la voix régulière sur la pénultième est une impression superficielle'. p.157: six lexical tone schemes; 'Le schème tonal I [(B)(B)HB] ... seule la première syllabe de la racine porte un ton haut ... peut être considéré comme canonique : il est de loin le plus fréquent et le plus proche d'une structure accentuée s
sources.locator: p. 148 (thesis), pp. 153-157 (six lexical tone schemes; scheme I canonical), p. 159 'L'accent du kikongo', p. 160 'Conclusion'
sources.note: The only dedicated study of Kituba word prosody; our record cites only a 10-page APiCS survey. It confirms lexical tone (six schemes, penult-H scheme I canonical, all-low and final-H classes) and adds that the length-accent is root-initial, not penult - worth adding as corroborating source and to sharpen the prule/srule wording.

sources.citation: Swift, Lloyd B. & Emile W. A. Zola. 1963. Kituba: Basic Course. Washington, DC: Foreign Service Institute. xxv+470 pp. (Glottolog 'grammar', id 35620; public-domain scan, no text layer; introduction scanned at 200 dpi)
sources.quote: 'In addition to the segmental phonemes listed above, Kituba employs stress and pitch differences. While not normally considered a tone language, Kituba does have a number of pairs of words the sole distinction between the members of which is a matter of stress and pitch.' sources.note: Glottolog's largest 'grammar' for kitu1246 (western/Kikongo ya leta variety, the one APiCS describes); pp. xv-xvi state the default 'accent on root syllable + pitch rise on penult' pattern with lexically low-pattern words and French loans as exceptions - independent 1960s confirmation of the record.

Laman (1936) l'avait déjà noté : l'énergie articulatoire caractéristique de l'accent dynamique du kikongo se localise en un point très précis à l'intérieur de l'unité lexicale : généralement sa place se trouve sur la première syllabe de la racine, quel que soit par ailleurs le schème tonal. (p. 159) — Conclusion p. 160: 'un accent à fonction strictement contrastive dont la place, toujours en début de la racine ou de la base lexicale, est, dans ce sens, totalement prédictible ; des tons dépouillés d'une part importante de leur pertinence linguistique'
sources.locator: p. 148 (thesis: eastern Bandundu variety is still a tone language; penult-rise idea 'une impression superficielle'); pp. 150-151 (H/L minimal pairs, falling tone, stable lexical tone); pp. 152-159 (six lexical tonal schemes; scheme I [(B)(B)HB] canonical and closest to penult accent); p. 159 section 'L'accent du kikongo'; p. 160 'Conclusion'
sources.note: First-hand analysis of the eastern (Bandundu, Zaire = DRC) Kituba, i.e. exactly kitu1246. Argues against Welmers 1973 / Lumwamu 1983 (who take vehicular Kikongo to be an accent language with a predictable pitch rise on the penult) that this variety 'est toujours une langue à tons au sens le plus strict du terme' (p. 148): two level tones H/L plus a falling tone, lexical minimal pairs (mbála 'sweet potato' / mbala 'time', mukóngo 'Bakongo person' / mukongo 'back', etc., p. 150), tones stable within the word regardless of syntactic function (p. 151), and six lexical tonal schemes (p. 156-157):…
